newsitem.title: USA: Telecom executives lured by start-up firms.
newsitem.headline: Telecom executives lured by start-up firms.

text.p: Top executives at the nation's largest telecommunications companies are being lured away by the challenge and the earnings potential of piloting small companies in this fast changing industry.

"I decided to take my chances in this big, brave world," said Richard Jalkut, president of Nynex Corp., who on Monday said he would be leaving the company after it completes its merger with Bell Atlantic Corp.
Jalkut joins a long list of those who have walked away from big corporations to seek new excitement and wealth.
"They are looking for the opportunity to make more money, to escape corporate bureaucracy and have a lot of fun," said Dennis Carey, a partner at recruitment firm Spencer Stuart.

The exodus of executives shows two trends, analysts said. One is the unique opportunities created now by the melding of communications, media, computing and software industries, and U.S. government efforts to crack open restricted telephone and cable television markets.
The second, partly caused by the first, is that the old companies are not so safe anymore.
New rivals, new markets, and mergers to meet competition are buckling the previously solid bedrock on which telephone companies were built.
No clearer example exists than AT&T Corp., which in 1995 began a split into three parts.

Even as the decision was being made, it lost chief operating officer Alex Mandl in August, and Joseph Nacchio as head of consumer and small business telephone units in December, both to small and relatively unknown companies.

PrimeCo, a national wireless company owned by Nynex and a group of other regional Bells in 1995, lost its Chief Executive George Schmitt, who took a half million dollar pay cut to join a smaller company, Omnipoint Corp.

Jalkut seemed to have good prospects too. He was to be president of the network group at the merging Bell Atlantic-Nynex, which would mean responsibility for running telephone service and operations from Maine to Virginia.

So now Jalkut -- who doesn't yet have an alternative job lined up -- says he would be interested in working closely with entrepreneurs in a small company, and getting paid directly in proportion to how well that company performs.
"That would be exciting," he said. "My individual contribution means more in the smaller environment than in the big environment," Jalkut said in an interview.

Carey said telephone company senior executive pay packages are typically in the $400,000 to $1.3 million range, excluding options and performance bonuses, having caught up with the market rate over the last five years.
But at smaller companies it is possible to become seriously wealthy, even though salaries are typically lower.
Big bundles of options or a chance to put up money for a stake before the company has its initial public offering all add to the gain.
In Mandl's case there was the extreme case of a $20 million cash bonus to sign on at Associated Communications LLC, and options which convert to an 18 percent stake in the new company.
